summary:
Manitoba is a province of Canada. Federal criminal law and federal human-rights protections apply here as they do elsewhere in the country, and the province's own human rights legislation and legislature operate alongside them.

The Manitoba Human Rights Code prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity. On 18 March 2025 the New Democratic Party government said it would amend the code to add gender expression as well. Justice Minister Matt Wiebe said the addition would bring Manitoba into line with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing. The change sits in a government bill before the Legislative Assembly, with debate expected later in 2025, and Trans Manitoba executive director Charlie Eau welcomed it.

Police-reported hate crime in Manitoba stood at 5.3 incidents per 100,000 people in 2024, the joint-lowest provincial rate that year alongside Newfoundland and Labrador, one of eight provinces whose rates were stable or falling. Police figures count only incidents that are reported to and recorded by police.

The Manitoba legislature passed a bill on 30 May 2024 designating March 31 as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility. It was brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a New Democratic backbench MLA for Kirkfield Park and a transgender man, who said the designation would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported.

In November 2023 the province raised the transgender flag in Winnipeg's Memorial Park for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, an observance it had first marked eight years earlier. The flag was raised by Oxenham, the first openly transgender man elected to the Manitoba legislature. Families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara said in a statement that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorialises people murdered as a result of transphobia, violence she described as showing no sign of slowing.
tangentialFactors:
The two recognition measures, the March 31 designation and the annual flag-raising, are declaratory. They create no complaint mechanism. The enforceable provincial route against discrimination is a complaint under the Manitoba Human Rights Code, which already names gender identity as a prohibited ground.

The provincial hate-crime figure is expressed per capita, which allows comparison with provinces of very different populations. A ranking by raw incident counts would follow population size rather than risk, and Manitoba's joint-lowest position is a comparison against Newfoundland and Labrador's rate for the same year.
localsOnly: The pending amendment to the Human Rights Code matters most to people living and working in Manitoba: it would extend protection to gender expression, covering preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing, in the fields the code governs. Residents' access to gender-marker changes on documents issued by the province, to transition-related health coverage and to school policies rests with provincial authorities; none of those provincial rules is described in the sources consulted here.
outOfScopeNotes:
The amendment to the Human Rights Code is not confirmed as enacted in the sources consulted. The most recent report is dated 18 March 2025 and places the change in a government bill awaiting debate later that year.

Police-reported hate-crime data cover only incidents reported to and recorded by police, and the categories include sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivation without reporting outcomes by victim group. The Manitoba rate was published by Statistics Canada and analysed in an LGBTIQ+ organisation's review of the national data.

No provincial count or rate of violence against transgender people was located. The November 2023 statement that transphobic violence shows no sign of slowing is not accompanied by figures, so no comparison against the province's general homicide rate is possible from these sources.

Manitoba-specific rules on changing a gender marker on provincial identity documents and vital records, on provincial health coverage for transition-related care, and on school policy for transgender students are not established by the sources consulted and remain unresolved here.
